from: a first weeks as a junior developer
to: running an engineering team and speaking for the firm to clients, vendors and review boards
case_setting: a named part of a software house
own_unit: a module, a release and a deadline
series_arc: first weeks as a junior developer → **running a team and speaking for the firm outside it**
learners: They work, or are about to work, in a Syrian software house, a product team, an IT department or a development shop taking work from abroad — where English is the language of the ticket, the pull request, the incident post-mortem, the service schedule and the messages that arrive from a client in Rotterdam, a vendor in Dublin or a security assessor in Zurich.
neutral: It is **role-neutral within the trade**. One cohort can contain a back-end developer, a tester and a support engineer, and all three practise the same skill on their own tickets and releases.
contexts_intro: The programme assumes learners work on different parts of a system, not one. Twelve software contexts carry the case studies:
contexts: Requirements and what the client actually asked for
Testing, QA and the bug that got through
Support tickets and the user who is stuck
upward: **Upward and outward paper:** tickets and pull request descriptions, incident minutes and post-mortems, estimate papers and change requests, decision papers for a director, standards a team follows, submissions to a client's review board, terms notes after a vendor negotiation and briefings written for three readers at once — usually written, usually read by somebody who was not there.
contact: **Client, vendor and assessor contact:** foreign clients and their product managers, cloud and API vendors, security assessors and auditors, contractors abroad, service review boards and customer councils, often where neither side is a native speaker.
reading_rows: Tickets, instructions, logs, messages, runbook pages — 133–184 words
Explanations, post-mortems, options notes, reports — 190–236 words
Decision papers, standards, submissions, hearings — 283–360 words
writing_rows: Tickets, notes, logs, a three-line handover — 48–74 words
Explanations, post-mortems, recommendations, monthly packs — 80–116 words
Decision papers, standards, appraisals, submissions — 145–184 words

posts1: Junior developer · trainee tester · support desk engineer · intern on a product team · junior front-end developer · build and release assistant · technical support agent taking tickets
gives1: Being understood on a stand-up and in a ticket, taking a requirement accurately, keeping a ticket and a log a second person can trust, answering for the team to a user, holding a rule under pressure, accounting for a piece of work and handing it on
posts2: Developer · senior tester · support lead · release coordinator · database developer · integration developer · client-facing engineer
gives2: Owning a module and a release: explaining a defect so a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on live code, explaining why an estimate moved, pressing a vendor, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen
posts3: Engineering manager · technical lead · QA manager · head of support · platform or infrastructure manager · delivery manager · deputy to a technical director
gives3: Other people's work and the firm's word: delegating, appraising, chairing the engineering review, writing the standard a team follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with vendors and clients, disagreeing upward, and answering a client's review board
constraint: a capable young engineer at the developer's grade

arc1_text: The learner arrives on an engineering team unable to operate, and leaves able to be relied on: to take a requirement accurately, keep a ticket and a log a second person can trust, answer for the team to a user who is stuck, be trusted with a release step and a code review, hold a rule under pressure when a client is pressing, account for a piece of work and hand it on.
arc2_text: The learner is given something of their own — a module, a release, a migration, a client's integration — and learns the language that ownership requires: explaining a defect so that a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on live code, explaining why an estimate moved, pressing a vendor, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen.
arc3_text: The learner becomes answerable for other people's work and for the firm's word. Three sessions are given to supervision itself — delegating, appraising and chairing — and the course runs on through writing the standard a team follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with vendors, clients and auditors, answering a client's review board, and arguing for the learner's own next post.
